messages.subject: Reactivity and Tabs
parts:
I've created a shiny app based off the 06_tabsets example. It's here: https://gist.github.com/4207364

ui.R defines one reactive input variable "n", and three tabs: A, B, and Plot.

server.R defines four reactive output functions:  afunc outputs to tab A, bfunc outputs to tab B, plot outputs to tab Plot, and foo outputs to the ether. All are dependent up on "n".

Questions regarding this app:

1. Why does the foo reactive function ever get called? Couldn't the client somehow notify the server which outputs it actually has? That way foo would never get run.

2. Clicking on the plot tab invokes the plot reactive function. Clicking to another tab and then back to the plot tab re-invokes the plot reactive function. Why? Toggling between tab A and B don't re-invoke their respective reactive functions.

3. You'll notice that there's a sleep call in the afunc reactive call, and it delays the display of every tab when "n" is changed, regardless of which tab is visible. Can the client somehow tell the server which tab is visible so that not all reactive functions dependent on "n" are called?

messages.author: f806781d102fe0ab
messages.subject: Re: Reactivity and Tabs
parts: 1. Why does the foo reactive function ever get called? Couldn't the client somehow notify the server which outputs it actually has? That way foo would never get run.
Yeah, it would certainly be possible to implement that.

2. Clicking on the plot tab invokes the plot reactive function. Clicking to another tab and then back to the plot tab re-invokes the plot reactive function. Why? Toggling between tab A and B don't re-invoke their respective reactive functions.

This is because one of the implicit reactive dependencies for reactivePlot is the size of the plotOutput's <div> on the page (unless you pass an explicit width/height to reactivePlot), and when you hide the tab the size goes to 0x0. If you set options(shiny.trace=TRUE) before running the app and watch the console as you switch tabs, you'll see this traffic going back and forth.

I made it work that way so that plots wouldn't render at all if their tabs are never shown. But you're the second person to bring up the re-invoking of the plot when none of the inputs have changed, so we might need to think harder about how to deal with this.

3. You'll notice that there's a sleep call in the afunc reactive call, and it delays the display of every tab when "n" is changed, regardless of which tab is visible. Can the client somehow tell the server which tab is visible so that not all reactive functions dependent on "n" are called?

Not automatically, but tabsetPanel can take an inputId which makes input$inputId reflect the currently selected tab, so your reactive functions could explicitly test if their tabs are visible and return NULL if not.

Okay, I've updated simpleTab to use the id, and I don't think this is the right approach. It may be my slow laptop but I don't think users will be happy staring at a greyed out tab that contains "NULL"  while waiting for the tab to "reactivate":

runGist('4221630')

I understand why it occurs; you've made the tabsetPanel id a reactive input upon which my output functions depend. Therefore they must be updated. However, there's got to be a better way to implement this in the javascript code on the client side.

 One approach is to use "differentiated reactive programming", as defined by the wikipedia article on "reactive programming", and set a higher priority on   propagating data changes to the "visible" tab first, then trickle in the changes from the non-visible tabs.

Or, you could just *not* send data to the non-visible tables until they're visible. This would definitely help the plot issue as well.

I'm going to peek underneath the shiny hood tomorrow and investigate.

messages.author: f806781d102fe0ab
messages.subject: Re: Reactivity and Tabs
parts:
Differentiated reactive programming is a very interesting idea. I would love to know if we could implement it practically.

1) Low-priority tasks would likely need to be interruptible as new higher-priority tasks are scheduled. I'm not sure how to interrupt running code in a "catchable" way with R, anyone have any ideas?

2) Reactive functions can have acyclic or even cyclic dependencies, in the general case it's not possible to assume that just because the reactive function that's assigned to an output has run and is now up-to-date, that the output is now ready to send to the user. You can see here[0] that we use a while loop to ensure that ALL reactives are up-to-date (length(.pendingInvalidate) == 0), and we don't send any output until we reach that state.

3) We would need to find a syntax/model that is accessible to R users, or at least, not make the current semantics any more difficult to learn or express.

I'm not trying to discourage you (or anyone else) from exploring this or other concepts, just pointing out some of the obstacles that would need to be overcome. The current reactive system is extremely simplistic (a good trait for a v0.1 of anything novel, in my opinion!) and we're definitely open to suggestions about how to make it fit better with real-world workflows.

In the meantime we have the manual workaround for "you could just *not* send data to the non-visible tables until they're visible" and I've been thinking about how we can make a targeted fix for #2 in your original post (I don't think it will be too hard).

[0] https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/blob/master/R/react.R#L96

messages.author: 48f24841e806e6c6
messages.subject: Re: Reactivity and Tabs
parts:
It's worth considering attaching a "visibility" or "active" attribute
to each output and only propagating data changes to outputs that are
"visible" or "active". Also, outputs can be declared to override this
attribute if it must be computed on every input change:

   output$plot <- reactivePlot(
function(){
      cat('output$plot called\n',file=stderr())
      plot(rnorm(input$n))
    },
overrideVisibility=FALSE
)

would only invoke the reactivePlot if the output were currently
visible.

An alternative would be to delay the propagation of the input data
changes until an output were visible.
